title: Suji halwa
subtitle: Indian semolina halwa with ghee and raisins
excerpt: Suji halwa is a warm, porridge-like pudding made from coarse semolina toasted in ghee, then cooked with sweetened water until it thickens into a soft, glossy mass. It comes together in about 20 minutes and is served hot straight from the pan. The texture is smooth, sweet, and faintly grainy, closer to a dense pudding than a dry sweet.
sourceNotes: Suji halwa (also called sooji or rava halwa) is one of the most widespread South Asian sweets, served as prasad at Hindu religious ceremonies and prepared for festivals, fasts, and everyday occasions across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and the diaspora. The same name covers a range of textures from the moist, soft-set version in this recipe to drier crumblier preparations. The technique of toasting semolina in clarified butter before adding liquid is also found in Greek, Turkish, and Middle Eastern halva traditions, suggesting a shared origin along ancient trade routes.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten freshly made; reheat with a splash of water stirred in.

content.text: Suji halwa is a soft, warm semolina pudding cooked in ghee and sweetened syrup. It takes about 20 minutes from start to finish and comes out glossy, aromatic, and comforting. The key step is toasting the semolina until it smells nutty before any liquid goes in, this removes the raw, floury taste and develops the dish's character.

Bring the water to a simmer in a small saucepan. Add the sugar and stir to dissolve. Keep the liquid hot over a very low heat while you toast the semolina. You want the liquid hot when it meets the toasted semolina, cold liquid can cause the ghee to splutter violently.

Melt the ghee in a medium saucepan over a medium heat. Add the cashews and raisins and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the cashews are pale gold and the raisins puff up. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and set aside. Add the semolina to the ghee remaining in the pan. Stir continuously over a medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes. The semolina will darken from pale yellow to a warm amber and smell nutty, that's the signal to add the liquid. If it darkens too fast, lower the heat.

Stand back and pour the hot sugar syrup into the toasted semolina in a slow, steady stream, stirring constantly. It will splutter and steam; keep stirring to prevent lumps. Add the ground cardamom. Reduce the heat to low and keep stirring for 5 to 7 minutes until the halwa thickens to a glossy mass that pulls away from the sides of the pan. Stir in the reserved cashews and raisins. Serve immediately in bowls.
